summary: A small archipelagic country in the central Mediterranean, once ruled by the Phoenicians, Romans, Arabs, the Knights of St John, the French and the British; it became independent in 1964, and its capital Valletta is a World Heritage Site.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Tradition holds that the apostle Paul preached in Malta after being shipwrecked there around AD 60, and Catholicism was re-established after the Normans reconquered the islands in 1091. The Knights of St John ruled from 1530 to 1798 and in 1565 repulsed the great Ottoman siege, and Catholicism became central to Maltese identity. The constitution makes Catholicism the state religion, and the festas of each village's patron saint remain the most important events of community life.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: In recent decades, with Malta's accession to the European Union (2004), economic development and the spread of education, society has gradually become secularized. The 2011 referendum legalizing divorce and the legalization of same-sex marriage in 2017 reflect the growing distance between the younger generation and the values of the Catholic Church, and the proportion of people with no religion has therefore risen.

ranking.name: Other Christianity
ranking.description: These include the Anglican Church left from British rule (such as St Paul's Anglican Pro-Cathedral in Valletta), Orthodoxy (immigrants in recent years from Eastern Europe and the Balkans), and other Protestant denominations. As a member of the EU, Malta has attracted many foreign workers, and religious diversity has increased.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: During Arab rule of Malta from 870 to 1091 Islam was the main religion, but after the Norman conquest Muslims were gradually expelled or converted. Today's Muslims are mainly immigrants and refugees from Libya, North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia in recent decades, and in the late 1970s Malta's first modern mosque was built in Paola.

religion.background: According to the Acts of the Apostles, around AD 60 the apostle Paul was shipwrecked in Malta on his way to Rome, and tradition holds that he spread Christianity on the island. In 870 the Arabs conquered Malta, and Islamic rule lasted about two hundred years; after the Normans conquered the islands in 1091, Catholicism was re-established. In 1530 the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V gave Malta to the Knights of St John (the Knights Hospitaller), and in 1565 the Knights repulsed the great siege by the Ottoman Empire, making Malta the "bulwark of Catholicism". During British rule of 1800–1964 Catholicism remained the faith of the majority, and after independence in 1964 the constitution made Catholicism the state religion. The 2011 referendum approving the legalization of divorce shows the gradual secularization of society.

language.official: The official languages are Maltese and English.

ranking.name: Maltese
ranking.description: Maltese derives from the Sicilian Arabic of the medieval period of Arab rule, and later absorbed a great deal of Italian, Sicilian and English vocabulary. It became an official language in 1934 and the national language after independence in 1964, and after Malta joined the EU in 2004 it became one of the EU's official languages; the great majority of Maltese speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English was introduced during British rule of 1800–1964 and became an official language alongside Maltese in 1934. English is widely used in education, business and government, and most Maltese speak it fluently, so Malta has also become a popular place to learn English, although those whose main language is English make up about a tenth of the population.

ranking.name: Italian
ranking.description: Italian was the language of administration and culture in the period of the Knights of St John (1530–1798) and was an official language until 1934. Because Malta is close to Sicily, many Maltese learned Italian through Italian television programs, but today very few people have Italian as their main language.

language.history: Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet, and derives from Sicilian Arabic of the Arab rule of 870–1091. After the Norman conquest Malta had close ties with Sicily and Italy, and the language absorbed a large amount of Sicilian and Italian vocabulary. In the period of the Knights of St John Italian was the language of administration and culture, and after 1800 British rule brought English. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries a "language question" controversy arose: the pro-Italian camp argued for Italian as the official language, while pro-British supporters and nationalists backed Maltese and English. In 1934 Maltese and English became the official languages, replacing Italian.

ranking.name: Pastizzi
ranking.description: Small diamond-shaped pastries of flaky dough filled with ricotta cheese or mashed peas and baked, with a crisp crust. Cheap, they are the most common everyday snack of the Maltese.
ranking.history: The origin of pastizzi may be related to pastry snacks in Ottoman and Arab cuisine, and they also resemble similar pastries in Spain and Italy, reflecting Malta's position at the crossroads of the Mediterranean. They are Malta's most popular street snack, inexpensive, often eaten at breakfast or in the afternoon with a cup of tea or coffee. In Maltese "pastizz" is also a common slang word, which shows its place in everyday life.

ranking.name: Stuffat tal-fenek (rabbit stew)
ranking.description: Rabbit meat marinated with red wine, garlic and bay leaves and then slowly stewed, with the sauce often tossed with pasta. The meat is tender and the sauce rich, and it is often eaten with fries or pasta.
ranking.history: Stewed rabbit is regarded as the national dish of Malta. During the rule of the Knights of St John, hunting rabbits was a privilege of the nobility and ordinary people were forbidden to hunt them. After Napoleon occupied Malta and expelled the Knights in 1798, the ban was lifted and rabbit dishes became popular among the people, so eating rabbit in Malta also carries a symbolic meaning of resistance to oppression. Today the fenkata (a gathering to eat rabbit) is an important tradition for family and friends.

ranking.name: Ftira
ranking.description: A flat round bread made from sourdough, split open and spread with tomato paste, filled with tuna, olives, capers and onion. It has a chewy texture with the aroma of tomato and olive oil.
ranking.history: Ftira is a traditional bread of the island of Gozo and the main island of Malta, and its method of making is related to Mediterranean flatbreads, the name possibly coming from the Arabic fatira. In 2020 "Ftira, culinary art and culture in Malta" was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list, the first Maltese item to be inscribed, reflecting its importance in the daily life of the Maltese.

ranking.name: Timpana (baked macaroni pie)
ranking.description: A large pie of macaroni mixed with meat sauce, egg and cheese, wrapped in pastry and baked. The crust is crisp and the filling rich, and it is a hearty main dish.
ranking.history: The name timpana shares its origin with the Sicilian Italian timballo, reflecting Malta's close relationship with Sicily during Norman and Spanish rule. Wrapping pasta in pastry was very common in the aristocratic cuisine of southern Italy and became a home-style dish after it reached Malta. Today it is often made for Sunday family dinners and festivals.

ranking.name: Bigilla (broad bean dip)
ranking.description: A spread made by cooking dried broad beans, mashing them, and adding garlic, chili, parsley and olive oil, eaten with bread or crackers. It has a creamy texture with the aroma of garlic and herbs.
ranking.history: The broad bean is one of the oldest crops of the Mediterranean, easy to grow in Malta's dry climate, and was in the past the main source of protein for the poor. It resembles Egypt's ful medames, reflecting the links between Maltese food and North Africa and the Arab world. It is often a snack to go with drinks in bars and also appears on Malta's traditional cold platters.
